newsitem.title: USA: House debates U.S. balanced budget legislation.
newsitem.headline: House debates U.S. balanced budget legislation.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives was poised to pass balanced budget legislation on Wednesday that supporters claimed would break Washington's long habit of deficit spending and give an extra boost to an already booming economy.
Just a day after President Bill Clinton and congressional leaders with much pomp formally announced a five-year budget deal, House Republican leaders pushed the measure to the floor for a quick vote.

"I am proud to inform the American people that our democratic process, something that has been maligned in recent years, is working," said New York Republican Representative Gerald Solomon. "Congress, working with the administration, can achieve fundamental goals."

The House planned to complete work on companion legislation on Thursday cutting taxes by $91 billion over five years. The Senate, which started debate on Wednesday, also hoped to vote on both measures before week's end.

Democrats, including some who supported the budget measure, complained Republicans were rushing debate before anyone had a chance to read the fine print of the massive legislation. They tried unsuccessfully to force a delay.

"I'm not going to vote for this bill because I can't even find the bill," said Ohio Democrat Marcy Kaptur. "What's the rush? Are you afraid the American people might actually find out what's in the bill?"

Despite grandiose rhetoric, the measure would not by itself balance the budget. It cuts spending by about $130 billion over five years, including interest, with the bulk of reductions coming from the Medicare health programme for the elderly.
It further directs Congress to find roughly $140 billion more in spending trims over that time period, but does not specify where the reductions should come from.

Critics charged future Congresses would never muster the political will to cuts in veterans, education, nutrition and other sensitive programmes needed to fulfil the political promises now being made.

"This is an Alice in Wonderland budget process. We're going to get to the balanced budget first by increasing the deficit with retroactive tax cuts," said Oregon Democrat Peter DeFazio. "Then, maybe later ... (spending) cuts will go into place."

Opposition has been muted, with Democratic and Republican leaders expecting the measure to pass handily. Analysts said even though the deal did not make major structural changes that will be needed to rein in mandatory programmes like Medicare it was an important step toward curbing the growth of government.
"The magnitude of the change and the direction of this legislative achievement is very great indeed,' said Florida Republican Porter Goss.
The legislation would reduce spending on Medicare by $115 billion over five years, largely by reducing payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers.

Beneficiaries would face higher monthly premiums for doctor's care, but would have an expanded menu of preventive health benefits and greater latitude to use managed care -- including tax-free medical savings accounts.
Medicaid insurance for the poor, elderly and disabled would be cut by more than $13 billion. Most of the savings come from trimming aid to hospitals serving indigent patients.
The measure makes smaller cuts in nutrition and education programmes. It calls on regulators to auction off part of the public broadcast spectrum, raising $21 billion.

In the midst of cuts, lawmakers made room for new initiatives, notably a $24 billion programme of grants to state governors to expand health care to many of the nation's 10 million uninsured children.
Negotiators were helped by a booming economy that shrunk the deficit much faster than expected, allowing Clinton to win spending and Republicans to secure major tax cuts.
